title: Words that are surprisingly from Arabic

entries.note: The Arabic dialect of Morocco, said to be the furthest from the other dialects, which makes Morocco a hard place to learn Arabic.
A modern adaptation of [[see:Classical Arabic]] drawing on all the dialects, understood across the Arab world but nobody's native language.
The form that [[see:Modern Standard Arabic]] is a modern adaptation of.
The Arabic definite article, still found at the start of many English loanwords such as [[see:alcove]], [[see:algebra]], [[see:alcohol]] and [[see:acton]].
One of many English words that still begin with the Arabic definite article [[see:al]].
Listed among English words that still carry the Arabic definite article [[see:al]].
Listed among English words that still carry the Arabic definite article [[see:al]].
Listed among English words that still carry the Arabic definite article [[see:al]].
Developed from [[from:alchemy]], and probably goes back to a Greek name for Egypt, where Alexandrian chemistry was practised.
Arabic adaptation of a Greek word probably meaning land of black earth, Egypt; the science of turning base metals into gold, which later became [[gave:chemistry]].
The substance alchemists sought for transmutation, from Arabic [[from:al]] plus perhaps a Greek word for a drying powder used on wounds.
From Arabic al-kuhl, the [[from:kohl]], a fine eyelid powder; it came to mean any distilled substance, then strong liquor, then any alcoholic drink.
Dark eyeliner powder, originally powdered [[see:antimony]], spelled differently from coal; it [[gave:alcohol]].
Most likely from Arabic, but mangled beyond recognition in Greek and Latin; powdered antimony was the original [[see:kohl]].
From Arabic al-qali, the soda or ash; first a salty substance, now a base that dissolves in water; it [[gave:kalium]].
Latin word for potash, from Arabic [[from:alkali]], which is why potassium has the chemical symbol K.
First recorded in the 14th century for useful minerals and now a cleaning product, from Arabic buraq and probably ultimately from Persian.
Shares its script and much vocabulary with Arabic but belongs to a different family; it was a prestige language, and its name shares an origin with [[same-root:Farsi]].
From Arabic, entering Middle English around the Crusades; it first meant padding worn under armour rather than the fabric itself; same source as [[same-root:acton]].
Suggested as a similar English word for the padding [[see:cotton]] originally meant.
English word for padding under armour, from Arabic al-qutn; same source as [[same-root:cotton]], with the a- coming from the definite article [[from:al]].
From a striped silk taffeta named, via French, after [[from:Attabi]], a Baghdad neighbourhood; it was popularised as a word for cats through [[see:Tabitha]].
The Baghdad neighbourhood where rich striped silks were made, which gave its name to [[gave:tabby]].
From a Persian word for silk or linen cloth, literally meaning spun or woven; [[see:tabby]] was a striped taffeta.
A woman's name whose association with female cats helped popularise [[see:tabby]], much as [[see:Tom]] was used for male cats.
Paired with tabby and [[see:Tabitha]] as a name for cats.
From Arabic za'faran; crushed stigmas of [[see:crocus]] flowers giving an orange-red colour, and a colour word used before [[see:orange]].
The flower whose stigmas give [[see:saffron]].
From Sanskrit via Persian narang, Arabic naranj, Italian, medieval Latin and French; the n was lost before reaching English, probably in Italian.
Medieval Latin name for the [[see:orange]], perhaps reflecting a folk etymology linking the fruit to the French town of [[see:Orange]].
French place name, as in William of Orange, [[unrelated:orange]] the fruit, though their spellings influenced each other.
From Latin praecoquum, early-ripening, via Arabic al-barquq and Catalan; related to [[same-root:precocious]], because the fruit ripens early; appears in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Related to [[same-root:apricot]]: precocious children are literally precooked.
Said to mean the apricot, making it a vegetable named after a fruit.
Reached English via Arabic sukkar from Sanskrit roots; its G sound is an unexplained softening of French sucre, like flacon becoming [[see:flagon]].
From Sanskrit via Persian qand, cane sugar, and Arabic qandi; it came from [[from:sugar candy]] after 'sugar' was dropped, and Americans favour it over [[see:sweets]].
From the Old French phrase sucre candi, entering English in the 13th century; the compound was later shortened to [[gave:candy]].
The older word the British kept for sweet things, where Americans use [[see:candy]].
From French flacon, a precedent for a C softening to G, as in [[see:sugar]].
Spanish for sugar, whose initial a- is the Arabic definite article [[from:al]].
Transliterated into English with either a Q or a K, with no consistency.
From the Arabic name for [[from:Pars]], since Arabic has no P sound; Farsi and [[same-root:Persian]] are the same language and essentially the same word.
Iranian region where modern Persian evolved, called Persis in Greek; its Arabic name [[gave:Farsi]].
Has an F sound rather than a P in Arabic, which connects it to [[same-root:Philistine]].
Connected to [[same-root:Palestine]]; the hosts debate its pronunciation, which Jess heard differently in church as a child.
From Turkish kahve, from Arabic qahwa, thought originally to mean wine; English's O vowel is unexplained. A rival theory links it to [[from?:Kaffa]].
Dutch for coffee, thought to have been borrowed from English [[from:coffee]].
Region of Ethiopia long known for growing coffee, proposed as the source of [[gave?:coffee]], though experts favour the Arabic etymology.
Its source is debated, possibly Arabic or Russian; countries that got the drink overland along the Silk Road call it something like chai, unlike [[see:tea]].
Countries that received the drink by sea tend to call it tea, while overland routes gave [[see:chai]]; an example of a [[see:Wanderwort]].
German term for a word with variations all over the world, like [[see:tea]] and [[see:chai]].
From Greek rhodon, probably from an Iranian root, via Latin, Norman and Middle English.
Western name for the [[from:Hashishin]] of the [[see:Nizari Ismaili state]]; spread by Crusader tales and [[see:Marco Polo]], its form was shaped by [[see:hashish]].
Derogatory name a Fatimid caliph gave the Nizaris; Europeans wrongly claimed they took hashish before killing, giving [[gave:assassin]].
Shia sect in mountain strongholds across Persia and Syria, 11th to 13th centuries, known for psychological warfare and assassinating rival leaders; Europeans called them [[see:assassin]]s.
What the sect's founder reportedly called his followers, meaning those faithful to the foundation of the faith.
In the 13th century he wrote of a young man drugged with a hashish potion and sent to kill, spreading the [[see:assassin]] story.
Not the source of [[see:assassin]], but it influenced the English form of that word.
Probably from imitative Arabic farfar, chatterer, via Italian and Spanish words for a braggart; a boastful sound, later rationalised as [[see:fan]] plus [[see:fair]].
One of the English words [[unrelated:fanfare]] was conflated with, though it has nothing to do with them.
The noise of the fair helped make sense of [[unrelated:fanfare]] as a loud celebratory sound, though the two are not related.
In the 1400s a blend of mercury and another metal; an alchemist's term from Arabic al-malgham, a poultice for sores, perhaps influenced by a Greek word.
From Arabic emir, commander, possibly plus [[from?:al]]; its D comes from association with Latin [[see:admire]], and its many spellings reflect ideas about its origin.
Its Latin source influenced the D in [[see:admiral]].
Title taken by Caliph Omar, showing that al- can follow amir, as the theory about [[see:admiral]] requires.
Like the D-less forms of [[see:admiral]], a Latin ad- word whose D was dropped in Old French.
French form of [[see:admiral]] with no D, because French dropped it; it entered English as a D-less variant.
First recorded in 1875 for a Sicilian criminal society; it is often traced to Arabic because Arabs ruled Sicily, but no convincing Arabic source exists.
Malta's language, a mix of Arabic and Italian, given as a comparison with Sicily's Arabic influence on [[see:mafia]].
Possibly from Sicilian mafiu, which may relate to Arabic marfud, rejected or outside society, though the OED isn't convinced.
From Arabic matrah, a place where something is thrown down, such as a carpet laid on the floor for comfort, much like [[see:sofa]].
From Arabic suffa, probably via French; in Spanish a masculine word ending in -a; in the Ottoman Empire, a more comfortable bit of floor.
Persian and Arabic, first a bundle of sheets or collection of poems, then an account book, customhouse and council chamber, and finally a seat.
Better called Hindu-Arabic numerals; a positional system that, unlike [[see:Roman numerals]], makes arithmetic easy and requires [[see:zero]] as a placeholder.
Used before [[see:Arabic numerals]], but they make adding and multiplying hard and have no zero.
Concept borrowed from Arabic mathematicians; the word comes from Arabic sifr, empty, through several European languages, and shares that origin with [[same-root:cipher]].
A more direct borrowing of Arabic sifr, empty or void, the same source as [[same-root:zero]].
Mathematician of the 9th and 10th centuries, rediscovered in medieval Europe; his name means 'the person from' a place, like Da Vinci, and gave [[gave:algorithm]].
From a Latin rendering of the name of the mathematician [[from:al-Khwarizmi]].

entries.term: The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing
entries.note: Book by [[see:al-Khwarizmi]], already discussed in their earlier numbers episode; its title gave [[gave:algebra]].
Literally means hanging together, so the hosts call theirs a compendious friendship.
From [[from:al-Khwarizmi]]'s work, meaning a reunion of broken parts, also used for setting bones; first a way to solve quadratic equations.
Medical term in Italian, Portuguese and Catalan for a bone setter, reflecting the original meaning of [[same-root:algebra]].
A mistranslation by [[see:Gerard of Cremona]], who confused Arabic jiba, chord of an arc, with jayb, fold or bosom, which Latin [[from:sinus]] translates.
Medieval translator of Arabic geometry into Latin whose confusion of two Arabic words gave [[gave:sine]].
Now the passages in the face, but Latin sinus meant any fold, bend or curve, including the bosom; related to [[same-root:sine]].
Every sense comes from [[from:chess]]; ticking things off and bank cheques come from counters placed on the chequered cloth of the [[see:exchequer]].
From Old French esches, chessmen, plural of eschec, from Persian shah, king; originally the Sanskrit game [[from:chaturanga]].
From Persian shah mat, the king is stumped, which passed through Arabic; mat was later misread as died, so it came to mean 'the king died'.
Original Sanskrit name of [[gave:chess]], referring to the army's four divisions: horses, elephants, chariots and foot soldiers.
From Old French eschequier, a chessboard; Norman England did its accounts on a chequered cloth, linking [[see:check]] to finance and government.
A medieval dice game named via French hasard, luck, from Arabic for a single [[see:die]]; its H is an overcorrection and its D comes from [[see:-ard]].
The singular of dice, which is what the Arabic source of [[see:hazard]] meant.
Jess's favourite suffix, a pejorative one, which influenced the final D of [[see:hazard]].
